findings.claim: Digital formats — compressed audio (e.g. MP3, AAC), uncompressed audio (e.g. WAV, FLAC)
findings.truth: FLAC is a compressed format. It uses lossless compression and cuts file size by about 40-50%. WAV and AIFF are the uncompressed examples. The spec (1.3.3) makes learners split digital media into compressed and uncompressed audio files, so the wrong example sits on an examinable distinction.
findings.evidence: spec 1.3.3 digital media formats; Wikipedia 'FLAC' (Free Lossless Audio Codec, 50-70% of original size)

findings.claim: A technician is responsible for setting up, operating and maintaining equipment ... An engineer operates the recording equipment and mixing console. Key fact: technician (equipment setup & maintenance). Flashcard: A technician sets up and maintains equipment; an engineer operates recording gear and the mixing console.
findings.truth: The spec splits the two roles the other way round for set-up: technician = maintaining and repairing equipment; engineer = set up of recording hardware and software. A learner taught this lesson would answer 'technician' to a question about who sets up recording hardware and software, and would lose the mark. The lesson also never mentions repairing, which is the technician's spec wording.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.1 Roles and responsibilities (technician / engineer bullets)

findings.claim: Vinyl records were the first mass consumer format.
findings.truth: Vinyl was not the first mass consumer format. Edison phonograph cylinders (sold from 1889) and shellac 78 rpm discs (from the 1890s) came first. The vinyl LP arrived in 1948 and the 45 rpm single in 1949. Vinyl is only the first format in the spec's list.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Phonograph record' / 'Phonograph cylinder'; spec 1.2 consumer audio formats list

findings.claim: Consumer formats in approximate chronological order: vinyl, cassette, CD, minidisc, MP3, music video, streaming. Revision tip: list the seven consumer formats in chronological order.
findings.truth: The order is the spec's list order, not a chronological one. Music video reached consumers in the early 1980s (MTV 1981, VHS releases), well before minidisc (1992) and MP3 (1993 onward). The key fact and its revision tip therefore drill a wrong sequence. Dropping the chronology claim is the surgical fix.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2 consumer audio formats (list order); Wikipedia 'Music video', 'MiniDisc' (1992), 'MP3' (1993)

findings.claim: Lower band (1-2) in the 6-mark and 8-mark mark schemes of all three lessons (6 mark schemes).
findings.truth: House band vocabulary is Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band. 'Lower band' is off-vocabulary and sits next to 'Lower-mid band' in the same ladder, which reads as two names for one rung. Renamed to 'Low band'.
findings.evidence: house rule in the checker brief (band vocabulary)

findings.claim: ADAT ... by recording 8 tracks onto VHS tape
findings.truth: ADAT recorded 8 tracks onto S-VHS videotape, not standard VHS. The point the lesson makes (cheap digital multitrack on a video cassette) stands, and no NCFE question can turn on the S. Recorded, not edited.

findings.claim: Which consumer format replaced vinyl as the dominant physical sales format in the 1980s? - The CD (compact disc).
findings.truth: CD unit sales did pass vinyl LP sales in 1988, so the card is defensible. It is still loose: the cassette outsold vinyl from about 1985 and stayed ahead of CD until the early 1990s, so the cassette, not the CD, displaced vinyl first. Left alone because the true picture needs more than one clause and the spec does not test format market share.
findings.evidence: RIAA / BPI shipment history (CD units pass LP in 1988; cassette leads from mid-1980s)

summary: Three lessons checked against the NCFE Level 1/2 Technical Award spec (v1.4, Nov 2025). One HIGH (FLAC taught as an uncompressed format), three MEDIUM (technician/engineer set-up duties reversed against spec 1.1.1, vinyl called the first mass consumer format, a format list drilled as chronological when it is not) and one LOW house-vocabulary fix across six mark schemes; 16 edits. No exam-claim errors: no lesson calls this a GCSE, names a paper, a tier, a board or SPaG, and every tariff (1-8 marks) fits an 80-mark 1 hour 30 minute paper. All 15 knowledge-check keys and all six answer keys per lesson recomputed and correct.
